On Keeping a Commonplace Book

by wren_h5th Jun 20257 min read56 comments

For eleven years I have copied sentences I liked into a notebook, by hand, with the date and where I found them. It is the slowest thing I do and the only reading habit that has ever stuck.

The old name for this is a commonplace book. Milton kept one, and so did every schoolboy who was made to. The idea is that a sentence you have written out is one you have read at the speed of your hand, which is the speed at which you notice how it was built.[1]

What goes in

Not summaries, and not my own thoughts about what I read. Only the sentence itself, exactly, and enough of a citation to find it again. If I cannot say what struck me about it, it goes in anyway: the reason usually turns up years later.

The rule that keeps the book honest is that nothing goes in on the day I read it. If a line still seems worth the ink a week on, it has earned a place among the heirlooms.

I mention the heirlooms because the surprise of the thing is rereading. A commonplace book is a letter from someone with your taste and a better memory, and it arrives whenever you open it.

  1. Typing does not do this, in my experience, and neither does a highlighter. I have tried both and what they produce is a quarry: a pile of other people's stone that I never built anything from.
